blocks.text: You already know individual pieces of this puzzle. You know int8 through int64 sizing from the NumPy dtype lesson, you know astype and category dtype from Changing Data Types. What you probably have not done yet is put all of that together into one systematic workflow you run on a whole DataFrame. That is what this lesson is about, measuring where your memory is actually going, then reducing it deliberately instead of guessing.

blocks.caption: Before optimizing anything, you need to actually know where the memory is going.

blocks.text: It is tempting to just start downcasting columns because it feels productive, but that is guessing. The first real step is always measuring, so you know which columns are actually worth your effort and which ones barely matter.

df.info() by default does not follow object dtype columns to see how much memory the actual strings they reference are using. It just reports a rough estimate based on the pointers, which massively undercounts any DataFrame with real text columns. Passing memory_usage='deep' gives you the true number.

blocks.title: Always pass deep for a DataFrame with any object columns
blocks.content: Without deep=True, df.info() can report a DataFrame as far smaller than it actually is, because it is not counting the real string data sitting behind each object column reference.

blocks.text: df.memory_usage(deep=True) goes further, giving you an accurate number for every single column individually, not just a total. This is how you actually find the real hog columns instead of guessing which ones matter.

blocks.caption: This is where you decide what is actually worth optimizing before touching anything.

blocks.text: You already know from the NumPy dtype lesson that int64 uses eight times the memory of int8 for the same values. pd.to_numeric() with the downcast parameter automates finding the smallest safe type across potentially many columns at once, rather than you manually inspecting each column's range and picking a type by hand.

code.content:
df["quantity"] = pd.to_numeric(df["quantity"], downcast="integer")
df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], downcast="float")

blocks.caption: pandas checks the real min and max in your data and picks the smallest type that safely holds them.

blocks.text: 3. Converting Low Cardinality Columns to Category
You already know the category dtype mechanic from Changing Data Types. The genuinely new question here is deciding WHEN it is actually worth doing, at the scale of auditing a whole DataFrame.

blocks.alt: Converting Low Cardinality Columns to Category
blocks.caption: Few unique values, many repeats. This is exactly where category dtype wins big.

blocks.alt: Converting Low Cardinality Columns to Category
blocks.caption: Almost nothing repeats here, so category dtype barely helps, if at all.

code.content:
df["status"].nunique() / len(df)  # a small ratio, great candidate
df["comments"].nunique() / len(df)  # close to 1, poor candidate

df["status"] = df["status"].astype("category")

blocks.title: Check the cardinality ratio before converting
blocks.content: A rough rule of thumb: if a column's number of unique values is small relative to its total row count, category dtype is almost always worth it. If nearly every value is unique, converting does little and is not worth the effort.

blocks.text: The most efficient way to save memory on a column is to never load it in the first place. usecols on read_csv() skips columns you know you will not need at read time, rather than loading the entire file and dropping columns afterward.

blocks.caption: Skip it at the source instead of loading everything and cleaning up after.
This works, but it wastes memory and time you did not need to spend.

blocks.text: low_memory, a related read_csv parameter, controls whether pandas processes the file in internal chunks while inferring dtypes, mainly affecting dtype consistency warnings rather than being a true memory solution on its own. For files genuinely too large to fit in memory at all, even after every technique in this lesson, the real solution is a different approach entirely.

blocks.caption: The next lesson in this module covers exactly this situation.

blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: Auditing and Optimizing a DataFrame
Take a moderately wide synthetic DataFrame and run it through the full workflow, measure first, then optimize.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Auditing and Optimizing a DataFrame
blocks.caption: One coherent workflow instead of scattered individual fixes.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Auditing and Optimizing a DataFrame
blocks.caption: A meaningful, measured reduction, not a guess.

items: Always measure with memory_usage(deep=True) before optimizing anything, df.info() alone undercounts object columns.
A per column breakdown reveals the actual hog columns instead of you guessing.
pd.to_numeric with downcast automates finding the smallest safe numeric dtype across many columns.
Category dtype is an excellent fit for low cardinality columns and a poor fit for mostly unique free text columns.
usecols at read time skips unneeded columns from the start, rather than loading everything and dropping later.
For files too large to fit in memory even after full optimization, chunk processing, covered next, is the real answer.
